title: Maitreyi's Question
hook: a wife is offered half a fortune and asks a better question
carry: atman: the self that makes anything dear
tomorrow: does a holy word live in the voice or on the page?

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma yoga: the act is yours, the fruit isn't. Arjuna set down his bow, and Krishna answered with Nani's line. Today, someone who turned down the fruits on purpose.
screen: `THE ACT IS YOURS. THE FRUIT ISN'T.`

segments.voice: A puzzle from one of the oldest Upanishads, the Brihadaranyaka. The sage Yajnavalkya is about to leave home and renounce the world. He has two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani, and he wants to be fair: divide what he owns between them. Most people would ask how much. Maitreyi asks something else. If this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich. So why would anyone turn the fortune down?
screen: `A SAGE LEAVES HOME.` → `HALF A FORTUNE.` → `WOULD IT MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` → `NO.`

segments.voice: Her answer is the key. What would I do with something that can't make me deathless? Tell me what you know instead. And Yajnavalkya, pleased, teaches her the heart of the Upanishad. It isn't for love of the husband that a husband is dear, he says, but for love of the Self. Not for love of a wife, or children, or wealth, or even the gods: each is dear for the sake of the atman. So the Self is what must be seen, heard, thought about and meditated on. Atman is Hinduism's word for the Self: not your personality, but the awareness underneath it. And the Upanishads teach that it is one with Brahman, the reality behind everything. Many teachers read Maitreyi's scene this way: everything we love is a doorway, and the love itself points deeper. That's why she can let the fortune go. She isn't rejecting what's dear. She's asking for the source of dear. It fits Krishna's line from yesterday: the fruits were never the treasure. And it's why Hindu tradition makes room, later in life, for loosening your hold on things. Priya has noticed something at Nani's. Nani is giving her saris to the cousins, and says she wants no gifts this year, only the card. Priya worried she was sad. Maybe she's doing what Maitreyi did.
screen: `WHAT WOULD I DO WITH WHAT CAN'T MAKE ME DEATHLESS?` · `ALL IS DEAR FOR THE SELF.` · `ATMAN: THE AWARENESS UNDERNEATH.` · `ONE WITH BRAHMAN.` · then, large: `THE SOURCE OF DEAR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind three people or things you love. One at a time, hold each one, and ask quietly: what in me is doing the loving? Don't answer in words. Rest with the question for a few slow breaths before moving to the next. If you pray, end by giving thanks for all three.
Devanagari: the script the Upanishads are printed in today, where atma, the Self, is one short word on the page.
Pocket this: the atman, the self that makes anything dear, the treasure Maitreyi asked for instead of the fortune. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Maitreyi's dialogue is a classic passage in Vedanta study, often read in Upanishad classes; Hindu tradition also names later stages of life, vanaprastha and sannyasa, for loosening one's hold on possessions and turning toward prayer and study.

fork.setup: a friend asks why your grandparents, now retired, give so much away and spend their mornings in prayer. what's a real Hindu answer?
options: tradition makes room in later life for letting things go and turning toward the Self, as Yajnavalkya left home to renounce.
it's just what people do when they get bored.
Hinduism says owning things is a sin.
fork.reveal: the later stages of life make room for loosening your hold. Maitreyi's question is the reason: wealth can't give what the Self can.

original.note: Sanskrit: the Self; in the Upanishads, the awareness beneath the personality, one with Brahman.
